title: Miketz: the Hanukkah portion
hook: Miketz almost always falls during Hanukkah: dreams and lights in the dark season

segments.voice: Yesterday, biladai: Joseph telling Pharaoh the answer wasn't in him. Your line was not in me. Who did you give credit to? Today, a portion and a holiday that keep meeting. Day two hundred eight.

Early winter, north of the equator. Dark by five. Cold car in the morning, dark driveway at night. And in window after window, small flames in a row, one more every night. That's Hanukkah. Hanukkah has fixed dates on the Jewish calendar, and the weekly Torah reading moves through the year in order, so the two keep meeting. The Shabbat of Hanukkah almost always reads Miketz, the portion of Pharaoh's dreams and Joseph's rise. Today: the Hanukkah portion.
screen: `DARK BY FIVE.` → `FLAMES IN THE WINDOWS.` → `MIKETZ MEETS HANUKKAH.`

segments.voice: First, the holiday. Hanukkah means dedication. In the time the books of the Maccabees describe, a Greek-Syrian king banned Jewish practice and set up an idol in the Temple in Jerusalem. A small band led by the Maccabee family rebelled, won, and rededicated the Temple. The Talmud adds the story of the oil: they found only one small jar of pure oil, enough for one day, and it burned for eight. So Jews light for eight nights, adding one light each night, as the school of Hillel taught, and set the lights where people outside can see them. Now, the portion. Miketz is full of dreams. Pharaoh's cows and grain. Joseph, who once dreamed as a boy, now reading dreams for a king. Seven fat years, seven lean, and a plan to get through the dark ones. Some readers hear a match between them: both are about light in a dark time. Hanukkah begins near the end of a Hebrew month, when the moon is thin, close to the longest nights of the year in the northern half of the world. And Joseph's story is a light in the dark, too: the prisoner forgotten for two years who ends up feeding the hungry from Egypt's stores. On the Shabbat of Hanukkah, the reading from the prophets is from Zechariah, who sees a golden lampstand in a vision. And in it, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit, saith the LORD of hosts." Dreams in the dark, lights in the dark. Neither one pretends the night is short. Each puts one small light in it.
screen: `HANUKKAH: DEDICATION.` · `ONE JAR OF OIL, EIGHT NIGHTS.` · `DREAMS AND A PLAN FOR LEAN YEARS.` · `NOT BY MIGHT, NOR BY POWER.` · then, large: `DREAMS IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a candle and recall a dream. If you have a candle and it's safe, light it now. If not, picture one, a single small flame. Settle, and breathe. Watch the light. Then remember a dream you once had for your life. Not a night dream, a hope. Maybe one that got put away in a dark year. Hold it near the flame for a while. You don't have to decide anything. Just let it be seen. The bell holds the time.
Miketz. At the end: the portion of Pharaoh's dreams, almost always read on the Shabbat of Hanukkah, with lights in the dark.
Your line: dreams in the dark. Tonight, when it gets dark, turn on one light on purpose, and let it remind you of one hope you haven't given up. Day two hundred eight.

howItsDone: Jews light the Hanukkah menorah for eight nights, adding one light each night, often in a window, with blessings; on the Shabbat of Hanukkah, synagogues read Miketz and the prophetic reading from Zechariah's vision of the lampstand.

fork.setup: you've found one small jar of pure oil, enough for one day, and you need eight. what do you do?
fork.reveal: the Talmud says they lit it anyway, and it burned for eight days. that's why Hanukkah lasts eight nights.

original.note: Hebrew: dedication. the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem.

trapdoor: what you thought: a coincidence of the calendar.
what it means: a portion of dreams and a festival of lights meet in the darkest season.
what a scholar hears: the Talmud (Shabbat 21b) records the oil story and the school of Hillel's practice of adding a light each night.

sources.quoted: Not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.

notes: 'Almost always' (Miketz on Shabbat Hanukkah) follows the index; confirm the calendar claim.
Hanukkah history is simplified (Antiochus IV, the Maccabean revolt, rededication around 164 BCE); dates omitted deliberately. Confirm.
Shabbat 21b (oil for one day burned eight; Beit Hillel adds a light each night; lights placed outside/at the window) from memory; confirm.
The Hanukkah haftarah (Zechariah 2:14–4:7) on the first Shabbat; confirm.
'Near the longest nights of the year for much of the world' refers to the Northern Hemisphere; confirm wording.
The practice invites lighting a candle only if safe; a Keeper may prefer not to associate an ordinary candle with the menorah.
